family.name: THE THING THAT IS NOT ON ANY LIST
family.one_sentence: A MAN TELLS A WOMAN OF SEVENTY-EIGHT IN A KITCHEN THAT A JOB ON HER GATE IS ABOUT TEN MINUTES AND THE FIGURE IS NOT THE WHOLE TRUTH, AND ON THE TUESDAY AFTER HE DOES THE EXACT SAME JOB ON A STRANGER'S GATE IN ABOUT TEN MINUTES, AND HE PUTS THE BRUSH IN HIS BACK POCKET AND DOES NOT GO BACK UP THAT ROAD, AND THE WOMAN WHO OFFERED TO DO THE GATE BUYS A BRUSH OF HER OWN BECAUSE SHE CANNOT ASK HIM FOR ONE, AND SHE DOES THE FIRST THING ON THE LIST IN FOUR HOURS AND LEAVES THE BRUSH ON A SIDEBOARD IN THE ROOM SHE SAID WAS THE ONLY ROOM ANYBODY SITS IN, AND THE WOMAN IT WAS BOUGHT FOR CANNOT ASK WHAT IT IS FOR, CANNOT BIN IT, CANNOT PUT IT ON A SHELF IN A PASSAGE, AND EVENTUALLY PUTS IT ON THE FLOOR OF HER OWN PASSAGE ON PURPOSE, AND THE CHAPTER IN WHICH THE GATE IS FIXED IS ALSO THE CHAPTER IN WHICH NOTHING AT ALL HAPPENS.

cards.0655: A man in his early forties takes the brush out of the bag in the footwell of his van on a Tuesday because he is on a stranger's gate with the same lump of old gloss on the back of the frame, and he does the exact job he promised a woman of seventy-eight in about ten minutes, and it is easy, and it is the easiest thing he has done in a fortnight. He has proved his own sentence out loud and he cannot say a word about it. He cannot go back up that road and admit it was ten minutes, because saying it was ten minutes means saying he knew, and he did know, and the only reason he said nothing in that kitchen was so that a woman would not have to be thanked. He puts the brush in his back pocket at half past twelve because he is going up a ladder and cannot carry the bag, and he does not think about it again until 0658.
cards.0656: A woman in her late forties buys a wire brush out of a bucket in a shop on the ring road on a Monday morning because she has a chisel and no brush and the drops on the back of that gate frame are one solid lump under old gloss, and she will not ring him and ask for one, because he will say yes, and because she has known since the sixteenth of July what she would do with a yes. She spends the whole of that Monday on a house she is clearing on the far side of the ring road with the new brush, which is a bad brush, on work that has nothing to do with any gate, and she does not knock at number twelve, and the reason she does not knock is not that the door would not open.
cards.0657: A woman in her early thirties from number ten, who taped a back room window in May and was told no in three seconds about a gate and did not ask why, walks up three doors on a Thursday afternoon and knocks, and the door comes away from the frame under her knuckles because it is not on the latch, and she goes in, and in about nine seconds in that house she is asked WHICH ONE and she says THE GATE, and she is out of the kitchen door and on the grass at ten past ten with a bag. She sees the sideboard in the front room on the way through and does not think anything about it. The two sentences she could have said on that step are a corner of brown tape and a chair, and she says the tape and does not say the chair, and she puts the roll into the woman's hand at the door and does not cross the threshold again, and she goes back down three doors with nothing in her hands. **THE CARD AS WRITTEN ABOVE SAYS SHE WENT BACK WITH THE ROLL STILL IN HER POCKET BECAUSE IT HAD BEEN HANDED TO HER. THE CHAPTER IS THE OTHER WAY ROUND AND THE CHAPTER IS RIGHT: SHE GAVE THE TAPE AWAY.**
cards.0658: The man in his early forties works out, in a unit at half past seven in the morning, that the brush is in the back pocket of a jacket on a hook and not in the bag, and that it has been on that hook since the twentieth of July, and he cannot work out how a thing got into a pocket, and gets there in about four minutes at a bench: he put it there himself on his knees on the ring road with a tread in one hand. He decides to do the gate. He goes to a shop on the ring road and buys a brush with his own money, because the one in the pocket is a stranger's and has a curl of old egg-coloured gloss in the crimp, and the shop is the shop with a galvanised bucket by the door that the woman in her late forties bought hers out of eight days before and neither of them knows. He puts the new one in the drawer under the bench in the van and does not shut the drawer, and he does not go up that road, and the reason is that the woman in her late forties put her hand over her mouth in a kitchen and said she would do it, and if he goes up there first he takes that off her and there is no way to put it back. **THE CARD'S *FOR A FORTNIGHT* IS A DAY-COUNT AND THE CHAPTER HAS NO DAY-COUNTS. THE BRUSH IS IN AN OPEN DRAWER FROM THE THIRD OF AUGUST ONWARD.**
cards.0659: The woman in her late forties knocks on a Saturday morning and the door comes in about a second, and she goes in, and the woman in her late seventies says WHICH ONE and she says THE GATE, and she is out at the kitchen door at ten past ten with a bag. She cannot get a bolster into the side of the lump so she goes at it from underneath on her knees in the grass and it comes off in about ten pieces in about two hours, and her hands are cut twice inside the palm, and the woman in her late seventies comes out across the grass at about twelve with a mug and stops two arms off on the walked-flat line and says *you'll want to put them back after*, which is the closest thing to a thank you anybody has said in that house since before Christmas. The bad brush is the thing that gets into the two-inch socket, because a short soft crimp can go where a deep hard one cannot. The gate swings and does not come in on the path for the first time since it was put on, and nobody is standing at it. At about half past three she comes in through the front door to wash her hands at the kitchen sink, which is at the back of the house past the front room, and she has to go through the front room, and she is carrying the brush, and the sideboard against the far wall is the first flat thing in a dark room, and she puts the brush down on it. **THE SIDEBOARD IS PLANTED IN THE MORNING, IN ABOUT TWO SECONDS, AND THOUGHT NOTHING ABOUT. THAT IS THE ONLY PLANT IN THE TEN.**
cards.0660: The woman in her late seventies has a wire brush on a sideboard in her front room and has had it since the Saturday. She works out first that somebody has been in her house, because the door is not on the latch, and then she works out that she cannot get at the fact because there is nobody to ask. She tries four places and rejects four places, and the reason she rejects all four is the same, and it is that every one of them is a place where somebody can ask her about it, and a bin is the only one she cannot get it to and you cannot bin a thing you cannot name. She tries the kitchen windowsill over the sink and it is worse because the sink is where she spends the day. She puts it back on the sideboard. And then at about half past two on the Monday she works out why she has not sat in the front room since the sixteenth of July: the room has a question in it, and if anybody comes in while she is in there she will be a woman being asked about a thing, and she has never been able to be that. And she gets the pencil out to cross off the first thing on the list and there is no pencil in the house, and there has not been since before Christmas.
cards.0661: The woman in her late forties has cuts inside both palms and does not go to anybody about them and cannot ask anybody about anything. She has four hours of gate work in her arms and no invoice and no money for it and a thing already delivered that nobody has thanked her for and cannot. And she has a wire brush in her own van that she bought for a job that is now finished, and a job that is finished is a job a tool has nothing to be for, and she puts it in the drawer under the bench in the van and shuts it, and the shut is the whole of the chapter. **THE CHAPTER ALSO CARRIES THE CUTS AND THE REASON SHE CANNOT DRESS THEM, WHICH THE CARD DID NOT ASK FOR, AND A GATE ON A SATURDAY MORNING AS THE ONLY WORD SHE HAD FOR A HAND.**
cards.0662: The woman in her late fifties at number nine, in from lates at ten past midnight with her sister at the table over a form from the council, is told without being asked that a light has been put in at number twelve, and then unasked that the woman of seventy-eight could not have done that herself, and she asks one question and it is only a place. She works out, standing at her own sink, that the man who has been in that passage is the man who made the stool she has eaten beside since the twenty-seventh of May, because a woman of seventy-eight told her on a step in May that he made it himself on a bench in a unit off the industrial estate. **THE CARD AS WRITTEN SAYS THE MAN GAVE HER THE STOOL. HE MADE IT. THE WOMAN OF SEVENTY-EIGHT GAVE IT, AND THE WOMAN OF SEVENTY-EIGHT HAS SAID NOTHING ABOUT ANY OF IT SINCE.** She works out that there is a thank you in it she can see exactly and cannot get at, and she cannot ask her sister one question, and she carries the stool out of the kitchen into the front room, because the kitchen is where you use a thing and the front room is where you look at one.
cards.0663: The woman in her late seventies empties the cloth out of the bowl under the bath tap in the dark at about ten at night on a Friday, points the torch at the bathroom ceiling by accident, and finds a soft brown mark about a foot across with a hard edge on it, and puts her thumb in it about a quarter of an inch and it comes back with grit on it. She goes up the stairs of her own house for the first time since the spring and finds the top landing in the dark and finds the hatch and the fixed ladder and gets a foot and a half higher on a stool from the front room and hears a high level cistern weeping at the far side of a joist, and does not go up the ladder, and cannot turn the supply off from downstairs because she does not know where the pipe comes up and never has. And she works out that the landing is over the front room, so the second thing on her list is the room the water is going to come into. **THE CARD SAYS *IF IT GOES ON FOUR MORE WEEKS*. THAT IS A DAY-COUNT AND THE CHAPTER SAYS IF IT GOES ON INTO THE AUTUMN.**
cards.0664: The woman in her late seventies decides on a Wednesday morning that the front room is now a room with a thing in it she cannot identify, and that she will not sit in a room like that, and that the only place a thing can live where nobody can explain it is where everybody walks. She puts the wire brush on the floor of her own passage at about half past ten in the morning, in the middle of the runner, with the handle across the walking line so that you cannot step down the side of it, and she does not wash it first, because a clean thing on a floor looks like a thing somebody has done on purpose. Then she goes out of the front door and round the side of the house and lifts both drop bolts out of their sockets with her fingers and stands the gate back against the wall of the coal shed, and does not go out into the road and does not shut it, and goes back in and shuts the front door behind her. There is no one in the road. **THE CARD SAYS A WEEK AND SAYS SHE LIFTS THE LATCH. THERE IS NO LATCH ON THAT GATE AND THERE ARE NO DAY-COUNTS; THERE ARE TWO DROP BOLTS AND SHE LIFTS THEM WITH A THUMB AND A HALF.** And she steps over the brush on her own way to her own kitchen, and nobody is standing in the road, and the front door does not latch and never has, and that is the whole of the difference between her and anybody else in this borough.
